text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Initial evaluation of tiredness, weight loss, darkening skin, low sodium and high potassium: blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid tests, ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate at the first visit; urgent 8 am cortisol and ACTH with a cosyntropin stimulation test within days; until then, salt freely, and go to the emergency department at once for vomiting, fainting, confusion or severe abdominal pain
  • Urgent endocrinology consultation within three days to confirm or exclude primary adrenal insufficiency, start replacement if confirmed, and plan the search for the cause
  • Replacement: hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking and 5 mg at 2 pm (15 mg a day) and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg each morning, adjusted by weight, energy, blood pressure lying and standing, salt craving and signs of over- or under-replacement, with sodium, potassium and plasma renin after any fludrocortisone change and at least yearly
  • Written sick-day rules (double the hydrocortisone for fever above 38 °C, triple it above 39 °C, and inject 100 mg and call 911 for vomiting, inability to take tablets, or feeling faint), an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit with training, a steroid emergency card and a medical ID, reviewed at every visit
  • Cause and differential: 21-hydroxylase antibodies at the two-week visit; adrenal CT and tuberculosis testing only if they are negative; examination for lymph nodes and spleen, LDH and a chest X-ray now, with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis if weight loss, fevers, night sweats or enlarged nodes persist once replacement is established
  • Screening for associated autoimmune disease: TSH (normal at intake) at least yearly; vitamin B12, A1c, and celiac serology with total IgA; ask about periods at each visit and check FSH if they become irregular or stop
  • Anemia: ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate at intake; repeat the blood count on treatment and look further only if it does not recover
  • Streptococcal pharyngitis: amoxicillin 500 mg twice daily for ten days; hydrocortisone doubled under the sick-day rules until a day without fever and then back to the usual dose; fluids with salt; the emergency injection with a 911 call if she vomits or cannot take tablets; neck nodes rechecked at the six-week visit

resource.title: Jane Austen synthetic care plan
resource.description: Recognize primary adrenal insufficiency in a 40-year-old writer whose tiredness, weight loss, nausea, back ache and darkening skin could be put down to overwork or low mood, and care for it on the Endocrine Society 1806 guideline: low sodium, high potassium and raised eosinophils as clues; urgent testing with an 8 am cortisol and ACTH and a cosyntropin stimulation test, without delaying treatment if she becomes unstable; renin and aldosterone for mineralocorticoid deficiency; 21-hydroxylase antibodies for the cause, with adrenal imaging and tuberculosis testing only if they are negative; lymphoma kept in the differential (examination for nodes and spleen, LDH, chest X-ray, and weight and symptoms on treatment) because a retrospective diagnosis of her real illness proposes it; hydrocortisone in two daily doses and fludrocortisone adjusted by blood pressure lying and standing, electrolytes and renin; written sick-day rules, an emergency injection kit, a steroid card and a medical ID, then used in a febrile illness; screening for associated autoimmune disease; anemia work-up (CMID anemia monograph); and listening to the patient's own written account of her illness. Her real illness remains undiagnosed; this record shows one modern possibility, not an answer.
